To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the identifiability of a union of languages from a class of languages is a decreasing function of the size of the class, and the number of languages in the union, and that the identifiabilty of the union of languages is a strictly increasing function of the identifiability criterion used.

the union of a fixed number of languages from a class is not discerningly identified by a learner if and only if the class contains a language that has an index in a class that is weakly reducible to it, and that there is an infinite hierarchy of classes where the unions of languages from the classes are discerningly identified, the classes are weakly reducibility closed, and each class contains a complete language.
the identifiability power of each of the three identification criterion decreases as the union size increases and that the discernibility criterion is more powerful than the other two.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identifiability of language classes in a union.
the following question: what is the power of inductive inference when the input consists of a union of up to n (fixed) languages from a given class?
the identifiability of unions of languages from a given class and we show how the identifiability decreases as the number of languages in the union is increased.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the union setting, the identification power of a machine decreases as we increase n.

, for each of the three identification criteria, there is an infinite hierarchy for the number of languages in the union, and the hierarchy is complete in the sense that there exist language classes which witness the hierarchy.

for any n and any identification criterion, there exists a language class such that all unions of up n languages from this language class are identified, while there is no learner that identifies all unions of n+1 language from this language class.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the unioned languages can be identified in a union, but the discerning identifiability of unioned languages is very difficult, even for simple classes of languages.
, in general, the more languages are allowed in the union of languages, the less the learner can identify the union.

we show that for every n there exists a language class where unions of n disjoint languages from the class can be discerned but unions of n+1 disjoint languages cannot, and that the discerning identification of language classes is reducible to the intrinsic complexity of the class.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in general, the union of languages can be much harder to learn than any of the individual languages.
in the unioned setting, it becomes harder to identify a language if more languages are allowed in the union.
, in the unioned learning setting, the number of languages that can be unioned is an important factor in the identifiability of the class.
